clue.text: Don't retire having got heavier, we hear?

indicators.note: what we hear is speech, so the spoken form counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: someone who has got heavier has their weight up

explanation.surface: Someone is told not to go to bed early, having put on a few pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retire' here means go to bed rather than stop working; staying up for someone is the sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay awake past bedtime, especially for someone returning, is the idiom; not retiring for the night means staying up.

clue.text: American tries as much as one wants

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for American
a go is a try, so two tries are two goes

explanation.surface: An American keeps attempting things for as long as they like.
explanation.walkthrough: A go is an attempt, as in 'have a go'; the plural is supplied as the word doubled.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived phrase means in abundance or without limit, typically of food or drink at a party.

clue.text: Lacking the brains to seize power, getting a little stick

indicators.note: to seize is to grab hold of, so one piece closes around another

blocks.note: someone lacking brains is too thick
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A dim would-be dictator tries a coup and ends up beaten with a stick.
explanation.walkthrough: TOO THICK takes P inside it, between the H and the I, to make TOOTHPICK.
explanation.definitionFit: The thin wooden sliver used to clean between teeth is literally a tiny stick.

clue.text: China protecting border lacking civilisation

indicators.note: something protecting another wraps around it as a shield

blocks.note: rhyming slang: china plate means mate, so a china is a pal
a rim is an edge or border

explanation.surface: China guards a frontier against an uncivilised region beyond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country, but in Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, so a china is a pal.
explanation.definitionFit: Primal describes something primitive or basic, belonging to an early state before refinement or culture took hold.

clue.text: Suffer embarrassment? If Bill will, he'll become ill!

blocks.clueFragment: If Bill will, he'll become ill!
blocks.note: surface reading: a man called Bill is warned that something will make him sick

blocks.clueFragment: If Bill will, he'll become ill!
blocks.note: setter's reading: the word Bill, dropping its front letter, turns into the word ill

explanation.surface: A question about embarrassment, followed by a warning that Bill will fall sick.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'face' of a word is its first letter: take B off BILL and ILL is left. That matches the plain definition 'Suffer embarrassment'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be humiliated publicly and forfeit respect is the idiomatic meaning of the phrase.

clue.text: Pub man defends around outskirts of Nottingham, showing who's in charge here

indicators.note: a defender stands guard on every side of what is protected, enclosing it
outskirts are the edges of a town, so only the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: your local is your neighbourhood pub
a gent is a man
to come around is to come over
the first and last letters of the city name

explanation.surface: A man at the pub stands up for the Nottingham suburbs, showing who runs the area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pub man' reads as a regular drinker, but the pub and the man are separate pieces. 'Here' points to the area where you live.
explanation.definitionFit: Councils administering a town or county are the authorities running your own area, as opposed to the national state.

clue.text: Moved confidently running dash, say, saving energy

indicators.note: running means operating or in motion, so the letters are set moving into a new order
to save something is to keep it safely held inside

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone sprinting for the line conserves their stamina and moves with assurance.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters SASHAYD take E before the final D.
explanation.definitionFit: To sashay is to walk in a showy, swaggering way, so the past tense means strode with self-assurance.

clue.text: Loud music is something put on for a party?

definitions.text: something put on for a party?

blocks.note: F is forte, the musical marking for loud
rock is a genre of music

explanation.surface: Loud music is what gets put on to get a party going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' suggests playing music, but here it means wearing; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress is clothing one wears to go out to a celebration, an example of party attire.

clue.text: Instruction for players playing soccer, letting in goal

indicators.note: playing around with letters means rearranging them freely
letting something in means admitting it inside

blocks.note: taken as written
an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: A coach tells the team how to play football, conceding a goal along the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' and 'goal' suggest football, but the players are musicians and the goal is an aim.
explanation.definitionFit: A score marking telling musicians to grow gradually louder is a direction given to performers.

clue.text: Flip out, having captured nothing on a chessboard

blocks.note: to have got something is to have captured it
O looks like zero, nothing
the chessmen standing on a chessboard are pieces

explanation.surface: A chess player loses their temper after failing to take a single piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Captured' and 'chessboard' make a chess scene, but captured is simply GOT.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose emotional control and break down is the idiom, much like snapping or losing it.

clue.text: War poet's opening words of Ode to London?

blocks.note: odes traditionally begin by addressing their subject with 'O'
Cobbett called London 'the Great Wen', a wen being a swelling

explanation.surface: A war poet is asked how his ode to the capital begins.
explanation.walkthrough: An ode to London addressed in the classical way would open 'O Wen!', using William Cobbett's old nickname for the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilfred Owen is the best-known English poet of the First World War trenches.

clue.text: Test party drinks husband put on ice

indicators.note: to drink something is to take it inside oneself

blocks.note: the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for UK vehicles
a ball is a formal dance party
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A trial party where someone's husband gets drinks served over ice.
explanation.walkthrough: The joined MOT and BALL take in H at the seam. 'Put on ice' is not about drinks but about postponing.
explanation.definitionFit: To shelve a plan or store equipment unused for later is the figurative sense, like freezing it.

clue.text: Fire pair of reporters lacking aspiration

indicators.note: lacking something means being without it, so letters go missing

blocks.note: a hack is a journalist, and a pair is two of them
aspiration is the breathy sound written H

explanation.surface: Two journalists with no ambition are sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' looks like dismissal and 'aspiration' like ambition, but it means the breathed H sound, dropped from both hacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ack-ack is old military slang for anti-aircraft guns or their shooting, from signallers' spelling of AA.

clue.text: Female ruler sought office in America and India

blocks.note: Americans say a candidate runs for office; past tense
I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A queen campaigned for election in both the USA and India.
explanation.walkthrough: Britons stand for office, Americans run, hence 'in America'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rani is an Indian queen or a raja's wife, a woman holding royal power.

clue.text: One commanding the faithful nanny to accept a charge

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: an ayah is a nursemaid in India
taken as written
a toll is a fee or charge

explanation.surface: A devoted nanny is persuaded to take on a new child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' suggests a child in care, but it is a fee here.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior Shiite cleric in Iran leads and directs religious believers, so commands the faithful.

clue.text: Suggestion made by public figure

blocks.note: overt means open, done in public
one is a number, a figure

explanation.surface: A proposal is put forward by a celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Public figure' reads as a celebrity, but splits into an adjective and a number.
explanation.definitionFit: An overtone is an implied hint or connotation beneath what is said, an undertone of meaning.

clue.text: Get a boost from Spooner's fish dish involving pastry

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner was famed for swapping the first sounds of words

blocks.note: hake is a fish; its opening H sound trades places with the T of the next word
a tart is a pastry dish; it takes the H sound in exchange for its T

explanation.surface: Someone's spirits are lifted by a fishy pastry dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the H and T sounds of a hake tart produces the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel encouraged and regain confidence is the idiom's sense, a lift to morale.

clue.text: Irish comic works gain ground

indicators.note: something ground is crushed and broken up, so its letters are reshaped

blocks.note: a mill is a works, a factory
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Irish comedian's material wins popularity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gain ground' looks like a phrase, but 'ground' is the past participle of grind, signalling a rearrangement; and a mill grinds too.
explanation.definitionFit: Spike Milligan, of The Goon Show, was a comedian who held Irish citizenship.

clue.text: What team's supporter will do in seat

blocks.note: supporters back whoever they support
a team is a side

explanation.surface: A fan describes what they do from their seat in the stand.
explanation.walkthrough: A team's supporter will back the side; 'seat' is not a stadium chair but the body part one sits on.
explanation.definitionFit: Seat is a polite word for the buttocks, which is what the answer also means informally.

clue.text: Ken from Edinburgh, say, uttered refusal

indicators.note: uttered means spoken out, so the spoken form counts

blocks.note: a refusal is a no

explanation.surface: A Scotsman named Ken says no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ken' looks like a name, but in Scots it is a verb, as in 'd'ye ken?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ken is Scottish dialect for to be aware or have understanding of, the same verb as the answer.

clue.text: Tipping over receptacle, leave cold drink

indicators.note: tipping something over turns it upside down, which in a down entry flips the order

blocks.note: a can is a container
to go is to leave
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

explanation.surface: Someone knocks over a container and abandons their chilled drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold drink' wants to be read together, but cold is just C.
explanation.definitionFit: Cognac is a brandy from western France, a type of alcoholic spirit.

clue.text: My hands holding a pen

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it gripped within

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
right and left, the two hands
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone holding a pen in their own hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is not a possessive but an exclamation, and 'pen' is an enclosure for animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A corral is a fenced enclosure for livestock, the same as a sheep or cattle pen.

clue.text: City founder dealing with problem arising

indicators.note: arising means coming up, and in a down entry going upward runs the letters backwards

blocks.note: re means concerning, dealing with
a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: The founder of a city deals with a problem that has come up.
explanation.walkthrough: Legend says Romulus and his twin founded Rome, so either twin can be called a founder.
explanation.definitionFit: In Roman legend the twins raised by a she-wolf established Rome, making each a founder of that capital.

clue.text: One dislikes the new mobile phone given royal honour

indicators.note: mobile means able to move, so these letters are free to change places

blocks.note: taken as written
the OBE is an order of chivalry conferred by the British monarch

explanation.surface: A technophobe who hates new mobile phones gets an honour from the King.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile phone' reads as one item, but 'mobile' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Neophobia is the fear or hatred of novelty, so a person afflicted with it shuns anything unfamiliar.

clue.text: Officially sanction the grade below A minus

blocks.note: B is the grade that comes after A
less means minus, as in five less two

explanation.surface: An official approves a mark of A minus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A minus' looks like a grade, but the minus is split off as a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To give formal approval or endorsement to a plan is a figurative use of the religious verb.

clue.text: Grand purplish colour, not soft blue

indicators.note: not here means without, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for grand
plum is a dark reddish-purple shade
P is piano, the musical marking for soft

explanation.surface: A grand purple shade that is not a gentle blue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' looks like another colour after all the purples, but it means sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue means being downcast or dejected, a mood the answer also describes.

clue.text: Drivel included in more naive policy proposal

indicators.note: to be included in something is to be placed inside it

blocks.note: green means inexperienced or naive
pap is worthless, trivial talk or writing

explanation.surface: A naive government plan is full of nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: A green paper is a British government consultation document setting out proposals for discussion before a firmer white paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The UK government issues these preliminary consultation documents to float possible legislation for public comment.

clue.text: Red head welcoming way to become a darker colour

indicators.note: welcoming a guest means taking them in, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: Che Guevara was a famous red, a communist revolutionary
nut is slang for the head
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A redhead's hair darkens with time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red head' reads as ginger hair, but Red is a communist, here Che Guevara, and head is slang for the skull.
explanation.definitionFit: Chestnut is a deep reddish-brown hue, a shade richer and deeper than plain red.

clue.text: Prune from France is sweeter than the others

blocks.note: to prune is to cut back
est is French for 'is'

explanation.surface: A French prune is the sweetest of fruits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prune' looks like the dried plum, which suits 'sweeter', but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet in the sense of charming or adorable gives the superlative meaning most appealing of all.
